newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER SHOWCASE-BARCA AND REAL LINE UP FOR CULTURAL CLASH.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-BARCA AND REAL LINE UP FOR CULTURAL CLASH.

text.p: Peace has reigned in Spain for over half a century but many of the tensions of the country's bitter Civil War will resurface on Saturday in the country's top first divisdion match between Barcelona and Real Madrid.
The fixture's non-sporting connotations make it the direct descendant of the feuds between Castille and Catalonia, two of the ancient nations that compose modern Spain.
So more than just being a sporting contest -- and one of Europe's biggest club games -- Barca-Real games pit together rival ideologies, histories, and even languages.
Real have long been the flag-bearers of the central area of Castille, and are widely identified with the intolerance of the Spanish right.
Barcelona, by comparison, are practically the national team of Catalonia, an area with a great medieval heritage and now one of the country's most vigorously independent regions.
It's a potent mixture in a country where separate nations have been welded together under rule from Madrid although the tension does not just belong in history.

Although much of the power accumulated in the Madrid ministries by the right wing dictator, General Francisco Franco, has now been devolved, there is currently widespread debate as to just how much decision-making should be made in Catalonia.

Much of the debate involves the Catalan language. Franco tried to smother the native tongue of Catalonia but it survived and even blossomed in one environment in particular -- the terraces at Barcelona's Nou Camp stadium.
Not surprisingly, there are now suggestions that Catalonia and the Basque Country should have their own 'national' teams.

Until they do -- and FIFA rules would have to be bent for that to happen -- the best comparison for a Barca-Real meeting would not be a club game at all but a "local" international such as England against Scotland.

In one legendary Spanish Cup clash Barcelona let in 11 goals in the Santiago Bernabeu stadium after allegedly being advised by the police that it would be best to lose in the wake of the Madrid fans' reaction to their 3-0 victory in the first leg.
For the Spanish public the effect of the clash continues to be intoxicating few people remain neutral.
Social events have to be planned to avoid the big game, which each year seems to clock up new records for television viewers.
And the media, for whom each fixture becomes "the game of the century", give the event a build-up worthy of an historic event.
With such a spotlight placed upon the game, supporters are quick to remember the perceived injustices of the past.
One fan writing into a Madrid sports daily reminded readers why Real Madrid have not won in the Nou Camp since the early 1980s.
"It's all down to the refereeing," read the letter, which listed a string of penalties, sendings-off and other incidents that he felt had been overlooked.
Not surprisingly, the repercussions of a one-sided game are enormous.

Graffiti reading simply '5-0' appeared all over Madrid after Brazilian striker Romario led Barcelona's drubbing of the old rivals in January 1994. A year later the score was reversed and the same graffiti moved to the streets of Barcelona.
Management at Spain's 'grandees' know that a good result in the old firm games can salvage a season.
Former Barca coach Johan Cruyff nearly lost his job early in the 1989-90 season but was saved by a 3-1 win over Real and went on to lead Barcelona to four consecutive league titles.

Most importantly for Barca fans, Cruyff also took the club's first European Cup, a trophy that Real had won six times. Their bid for a seventh consecutive title had ended in the second round -- at the hands of Barca.
Cruyff was also at the centre of probably the most famous Barcelona victory ever -- the 5-0 drubbing of Real in Madrid's Santiago Bernabeu stadium in 1974.
And when, several years later, the Madrid-based Spanish national television company announced that it had lost the footage of the game, Catalan fans were quick to smell a rat.
